newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo army puts down mutiny, detains mutineers.
newsitem.headline: Congo army puts down mutiny, detains mutineers.

text.p: Congo's army said on Thursday it had put down a mutiny within its ranks by former political militiamen who cut a major rail link and deprived the country's economic capital Pointe-Noire of power.

Chief of Staff General Daniel Mabika told a news conference late on Thursday that the 100 or so mutineers at the Loudima army training centre 350 km (240 miles) south west of the capital Brazzaville would be tried by senior officers.
He said nine people had been slightly wounded in the operation to curb the mutiny, launched on Saturday by former militia supporters of President Pascal Lissouba.
"All has returned to normal after the army used force and succeeded in restoring the electricity," Mabika said, warning that "any future mutinies will be put down whatever quarter they came from".

The Loudima mutiny was the third by ex-militiamen promised places in the army under a deal to end political and ethnic unrest that killed 2,000 people in Brazzaville's southern suburbs following disputed parliamentary elections in 1993.
The mutineers demanded the sacking of their commander and immediate integration into the army with the rank of sergeant.

No action was taken against mutineers who staged revolts in 1995 and 1996 inside their barracks but Mabika said the latest mutineers had gone too far by attacking the oil-producing nation's economic interests.
They had blocked the rail link between the capital and Pointe-Noire and halted a power station supplying the economic capital and the Central African nation's third town of Dolisie.
Congo, which suffered a turbulent transition to democracy in the early 1990s, faces presidential elections in July with over half a dozen rivals already jostling to take on Lissouba.
